stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.6 key concept: changes in food production, population growth, and industrialization led to migration
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing causes of migration, 1840–1914
stimulusBlocks.text:
Between 1840 and 1914, tens of millions of Europeans left their homelands. Some fled disaster: during the Irish famine of 1845 to 1852, about a million people died and more than a million emigrated. Others left because farmland was scarce as population grew, or because industrial jobs paid more in the Americas.

Steamships and railroads made migration cheaper and faster. Letters and money sent home by earlier migrants encouraged relatives to follow.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, which of the following made migration cheaper and faster?
questions.explanation: The passage names steamships and railroads.
choiceExplanations: The passage names steamships and railroads.
questions.distinguisher: Steam, not sail, made travel cheaper and faster.

stimulusBlocks.source: CED Topic 6.6 key concept: migrants included indentured servants, such as South Asian and Chinese laborers, who worked on plantations and in mines after the end of slavery
stimulusBlocks.attribution: Practice passage written for Page One, summarizing indentured labor migration, 1834–1917
stimulusBlocks.text:
After Britain abolished slavery in 1833, plantation owners in the Caribbean, Mauritius, Fiji, and southern Africa needed new workers. More than a million laborers from India signed contracts of indenture, agreeing to work for a set number of years, usually five, in exchange for passage, wages, and sometimes a return ticket. Chinese laborers went under similar contracts to Cuba, Peru, and Southeast Asia.

Indentured workers were not enslaved, but many faced harsh conditions, low pay, and penalties for leaving their employers. Many stayed after their contracts ended and formed lasting communities.
